title: Is Lichtenstein an actual monarchy? - Marginal REVOLUTION
gist: The Princely House of Liechtenstein quietly approved changes to its House Law that further concentrate power in Prince Alois — expanding his discretion over dynasty membership, titles, and pardons — approved solely by the dynasty itself rather than parliament or the public.

themes.theme: Concentration of dynastic power in Liechtenstein

insights.claim: The Princely House of Liechtenstein quietly approved an overhaul of its House Law that strengthens the authority of Prince Alois, who already wields extraordinary power over the country's roughly 42,000 citizens, while reducing checks previously held by his relatives.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Liechtenstein is a significant private-banking and wealth-management jurisdiction; increased concentration of unilateral princely authority over dynastic and legal matters is a governance-risk data point for entities with exposure there.
insights.quote: Europe's wealthiest ruling dynasty had quietly approved an overhaul that strengthens the authority of a prince who already wields extraordinary power over his 42,000 citizens

insights.claim: Even before the latest changes, Prince Alois already held the power to veto legislation, dismiss the government, dissolve parliament, appoint judges, and reject laws approved by a referendum — including vetoing, in June 2026, a citizens' initiative to legalize abortion within the first 12 weeks even if voters approved it.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Illustrates that Liechtenstein's constitutional monarchy already grants near-absolute veto power to the prince over democratic outcomes, relevant context for assessing political/regulatory risk in the jurisdiction.
insights.quote: In June, the Catholic prince said he would veto a citizens' initiative to legalise abortion during the first 12 weeks of pregnancy, even if voters backed it…

insights.claim: Under the new House Law changes, the prince gains greater discretion over who belongs to the dynasty and explicit authority to set rules on family names, titles, and coats of arms, while the Family Council — expanded from three to five members — loses its previous check of needing to consent to pardons.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: A weakening of internal dynastic checks-and-balances even as the council's nominal size grows, a pattern worth noting for anyone evaluating Liechtenstein's institutional governance stability.
insights.quote: the prince will no longer need its consent for pardons, only to consult it…

insights.claim: The reforms to Liechtenstein's House Law were approved entirely by members of the ruling dynasty itself, with no involvement from parliament or the public.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Highlights that Liechtenstein's core governance rules can be altered unilaterally by the ruling family, a structural feature relevant to long-horizon political-risk assessment of the jurisdiction.
insights.quote: The reforms were approved not by parliament or the public, but by members of the dynasty itself.
